---
title: "ATen tokenization"
---

Cellerator's optional tokenization component transforms caller-defined features
and event occurrences into sequences. ATen owns tensor storage, devices, views
and dtypes. Numerical operations remain reusable independently of tokenization.
The component does not depend on Cellerator's CUDA-mechanism Torch adapter.

## Build and Python installation

Select a matching Torch installation for the C++ library and Python interpreter:

```sh
cmake -S . -B build/tokenization-cpu \
  -DCELLERATOR_ENABLE_CUDA=OFF \
  -DCELLERATOR_ENABLE_TOKENIZATION=ON \
  -DCELLERATOR_ENABLE_PYTHON=ON \
  -DCELLERATOR_BUILD_PRODUCT2=ON \
  -DPython_EXECUTABLE=/path/to/python \
  -Dpybind11_DIR="$(/path/to/python -m pybind11 --cmakedir)"
cmake --build build/tokenization-cpu --target cellerator_python_extensions -j2
```

Use CPU libtorch for a configuration without CUDA dependencies. A CUDA-enabled
Torch package can require the CUDA toolkit even when executing CPU tensors.
For CUDA kernels, enable `CELLERATOR_ENABLE_CUDA=ON` with a compatible CUDA
Torch package and explicit `CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES`.

Build/install the Python package against the interpreter's existing Torch:

```sh
/path/to/python -m pip install --no-build-isolation . \
  --config-settings=cmake.define.CELLERATOR_ENABLE_TOKENIZATION=ON
```

Add `--config-settings=cmake.define.CELLERATOR_ENABLE_CUDA=ON` for CUDA append.
Install build dependencies (`scikit-build-core` and `pybind11`) and Torch into
that interpreter first. The default package remains independent of libtorch;
request tokenization explicitly. No general migration of existing native
runtime buffers is performed by enabling this component.

Installed C++ consumers use:

```cmake
find_package(Cellerator CONFIG REQUIRED COMPONENTS tokenization)
target_link_libraries(my_target PRIVATE Cellerator::tokenization)
```

Consumers needing only numerical operations request the `aten_ops` component
and link `Cellerator::aten_ops`. These C++ targets do not link `torch_python`.

## Representation and identity

`Vocabulary` maps unique caller-defined integer identities to nonnegative token
IDs. Build symbolic-label dictionaries at the caller boundary; keep feature
identities explicit when columns are reordered. Move prepared vocabularies to
the selected device explicitly. Unknown identities are errors by default;
dropping them or using an explicit unknown token is a caller decision.

`TokenBatch` contains flat `int64` token IDs, `int64` offsets delimiting each
sequence, and named attribute tensors shaped `[occurrences, ...]`. Attributes
retain their dtype and move with their occurrences. Names such as `time`,
`measurement` or `provenance` do not acquire built-in semantics. Empty sequences
are represented by repeated offsets. Repeated token IDs are valid.

Packing and padding preserve sequence boundaries and attribute alignment.
`add_boundaries` accepts caller-created prefix/suffix batches with explicit
attribute values, so the library does not invent special-token metadata.

## Ranked features and numerical operations

`ranked_feature` accepts dense `[observations, features]` or canonical CSR
tensors, explicitly aligned unique feature identities and a vocabulary. CSR
columns must be sorted and unique within each row. Unstored entries are zero;
explicit zeros are ineligible by default. General nonzero measurements may be
negative. A supplied eligibility mask restricts the original nonzero support.

Caller-supplied scores determine descending rank; otherwise measurements are
scores. Equal scores are ordered by ascending feature identity, including at
the truncation boundary. Output can retain measurements, scores and arbitrary
aligned attributes. Sparse ranking operates on stored entries without a dense
observation-by-feature intermediate.

`normalize_features`, `select_ranked_features` and `nonzero_feature_median`
belong to the separate ATen numerical layer. Compose normalization before
ranking to supply another scoring convention. Real arithmetic uses FP32 for
half/BF16/FP32/integer input and FP64 for FP64 input, with explicit FP64
computation available. Normalization preserves floating storage dtype; promote
the input explicitly when FP32 or FP64 normalized scores must retain precision.

Median fitting accepts supplied dense/CSR batches sharing a feature axis and
device. It excludes zero measurements, uses the mean of the two middle values
for even counts, and returns NaN/zero/false for empty-feature median/count/validity.
Feature blocking bounds temporary memory. Corpus choice, input normalization,
gene alias aggregation and persistent reference-statistics storage are caller
responsibilities.

The `geneformer_style` profile calculates
`score[c,g] = counts[c,g] / total_counts[c] * 10000 / feature_medians[g]`.
It accepts nonnegative measurements, retains positive expressed features and
uses fixed supplied reference factors. Total counts are supplied independently
of vocabulary filtering. Empty observations yield empty sequences.
The profile uses FP32 arithmetic unless counts are FP64; its `compute_type`
option accepts `"float32"` or `"float64"` for an explicit choice. Use FP64 for
upstream formula comparisons where rounding could change feature ordering.

This implements a Geneformer-style profile rather than all upstream dataset
processing. Compare the supported formula against the
[upstream tokenizer](https://geneformer.readthedocs.io/en/latest/_modules/geneformer/tokenizer.html).
Gene-ID collapsing, model-specific vocabulary artifacts, special tokens and
sequence lengths remain explicit caller inputs. Ties use Cellerator's stable
identity rule; upstream NumPy sorting and different arithmetic precision may
order ties and near-ties differently.

## Event streams and incremental storage

`event_stream` encodes supplied event identities while retaining their order,
repetitions and attributes. It does not detect events, infer causal order, sort
timestamps, or interpret an injected occurrence as a causal intervention.
The Karyoplast example starts with already-defined positive gene events.

`SequenceBuffer` owns ATen storage with explicit per-sequence capacities,
current lengths and an attribute schema. `append_into` updates selected rows
and returns device-resident success flags. Pass a reusable `status_buffer` bool
tensor aligned to selected rows to avoid allocating status on each append;
its contents are overwritten on the next use. A row that cannot accommodate its
update is unchanged. `append_checked` additionally checks success on the host;
other successful rows may already have advanced when an overflow is reported.
`reserve` explicitly creates larger storage while preserving current contents.
No operation automatically evicts events or chooses a model history window.

The bounded append path writes only new payload, retains tensor ownership, and
does not copy previous history or read lengths back to the host each step.
Compact encoding, validation and `compact()` can synchronize to determine
data-dependent output sizes. Encoding-into convenience functions compose
encoding with append and may inherit the encoding synchronization costs.
They are distinct from appending already-encoded batches on the fast path.
Storage accessors return borrowed tensor views; treat lengths as read-only.
Append, compaction and reserve validate length bounds before using them.

Pure normalization and attribute gathers retain ordinary ATen differentiation;
discrete identity/rank choices do not have gradients. Mutable append is for
inference/storage and rejects gradient-tracked payloads. CUDA operations use the
current stream on the tensor's device; callers establish ordering across
streams and must not concurrently mutate the same buffer.

## Scientific ownership and qualification

Karyoplast determines what an event means and how observations produce it.
Cytoplast owns environment and population execution. Intervention semantics,
lifecycle commands, history windows, model state and daughter-state inheritance
are not tokenizer protocols. Embeddings remain separate from tokenization.

Run the numerical/core/append CTests and the independent Python suite under
`tests/tokenization`. The benchmark driver under `bench/tokenization` requires
an explicit device and compares an ATen baseline. GPU tests, sanitizers and
timing require admitted Device Scheduler execution. Qualification results and
environment limits are recorded separately; CPU success does not qualify CUDA
correctness, performance or scientific validity.

## HPC CUDA and profiling

PyTorch's CUDA runtime package and the CUDA development toolkit serve different
roles. Build Cellerator's CUDA kernels with the selected HPC toolkit's `nvcc`
and use its Nsight and Compute Sanitizer tools to inspect execution. Source
mapping requires `CELLERATOR_ENABLE_CUDA_LINEINFO=ON`.

On this host the explicit compiler is
`/opt/nvidia/hpc_sdk/Linux_x86_64/26.1/cuda/12.9/bin/nvcc`, with
`CMAKE_CUDA_HOST_COMPILER=/usr/bin/g++-12` and
`CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=70` for V100. The installed PyTorch 2.7 package uses
CUDA runtime 12.6. Compatibility is qualified by compilation and admitted
execution; matching toolkit/runtime major versions alone is not qualification.
Use the finite `bench/tokenization/profile_smoke.py` workload inside a scheduler
job for Nsight Systems tracing or a bounded Nsight Compute kernel capture.

In the qualified installation, generic HPC `compilers/bin` profiler wrappers
defaulted to an absent CUDA 13.1 tool tree. Use these installed CUDA 12.9 tools
explicitly rather than changing the global toolkit configuration:

- `/opt/nvidia/hpc_sdk/Linux_x86_64/26.1/cuda/12.9/compute-sanitizer/compute-sanitizer`
- `/opt/nvidia/hpc_sdk/Linux_x86_64/26.1/profilers/12.9/Nsight_Systems_2025.3/target-linux-x64/nsys`
- `/opt/nvidia/hpc_sdk/Linux_x86_64/26.1/profilers/12.9/Nsight_Compute/ncu`
